leads.candidate: Dumbarton Oaks / Dumbarton Oaks Park veteran trees, and the Montrose Park Tulip Poplar (HALS DC-?, tile.loc.gov/.../dc1036), Georgetown
leads.why_a_lead: Unchanged from the prior pass for Dumbarton Oaks itself (still not surfaced by open web search; would need doaks.org library-archives plant lists directly). NEW this pass: the Montrose Park Tulip Poplar is confirmed as a distinct, separate HALS witness tree record (dc1036, 'Montrose Park Tulip Poplar, Montrose Park, clearing in northwest corner, Washington, DC') found via web search of the HALS numbering sequence, but www.loc.gov blocks curl/WebFetch with a Cloudflare challenge and the tile.loc.gov PDF for dc1036 returned 403 this pass (unlike dc1027/1028/1029/1030/1034/1039/1040 which returned the PDF fine), so its content is still unverified. Montrose Park is a free, fully public NPS-adjacent Georgetown park directly next to Dumbarton Oaks Park, so the two would form a natural second Georgetown cluster if both pan out. A future pass should retry the dc1036 PDF (transient 403s happened on this host) and search for the tulip poplar by name plus a second source.

leads.candidate: Andrew Jackson Magnolia(s), White House South Portico
leads.why_a_lead: UPDATED this pass via the National Park Trust blog (parktrust.org, independent second source, corroborates the NPS 'Silent Sentinels' article): confirms one tree was radically cut back in 2018 due to age/decline (not fully removed in 2017 as an earlier pass understood); the blog states 'still reportedly there today' as of its own (recent, copyright 2026) writing, having watched 39 presidencies, with a seedling from the original standing by for eventual succession. This resolves part of the earlier open question about which of the two trees survives, but the access question is UNCHANGED and still blocking: the White House South Lawn is not general public access, and this pass still could not confirm whether the tree is visible from the public Ellipse/E Street or only from inside ticketed tours. Needs an access check before it could ever ship, per hard rule 10 on withheld/restricted locations.

leads.candidate: 1910 Japanese Flowering Cherry Trees, East Potomac Golf Course (HALS DC-8, tile.loc.gov/.../dc1034)
leads.why_a_lead: Same 2006 HALS Witness Tree Protection Program as wdc_001/004/006/008/009/010. This pass downloaded the HALS PDF (tile.loc.gov/storage-services/master/pnp/habshaer/dc/dc1000/dc1034/data/dc1034data.pdf, 342KB) but it is a scanned image (JBIG2) with no extractable text and no OCR tool available this pass, so its documented health flag ('hollow condition of most principal branches consistent with past insect infestation', per the LOC item title/metadata found via web search) could not be verified in detail or dated. Also an ensemble ('cherry trees', plural, at a golf course, not one obvious standing point) that needs a collectible-point judgement call. A future pass with OCR/PDF-reading capability, or a session that can view www.loc.gov/pictures/item/dc1034 directly (blocked by Cloudflare to curl and WebFetch this pass, tile.loc.gov PDF host works fine), should resolve both the health question and whether this counts as one collectible point.

leads.candidate: Frederick Douglass White Oak, Cedar Hill (HALS DC-?, tile.loc.gov/.../dc1028, 'Frederick Douglass White Oak, 1411 West Street SE, Northeast of front porch')
leads.why_a_lead: Strong candidate on paper: single named tree, NPS-owned National Historic Site (Frederick Douglass NHS, Cedar Hill, Anacostia), part of the same HALS programme, described elsewhere as the largest tree remaining from Douglass's own time on the property. NOT pursued to verification this pass for two reasons: (1) time budget went to the Mall/Tidal Basin cluster per this pass's brief, since Cedar Hill is a separate site in Anacostia, SE DC, roughly 20-25 min from downtown, that would not join the existing wdc_002/004/005 walk; (2) this pass could not find a source confirming the specific named witness tree is still standing as opposed to oaks in general still being present on the knoll (TCLF's Cultural Landscape Foundation page, https://www.tclf.org/frederick-douglass-national-historic-site, confirms 'the knoll is dominated by lawn and crowned with numerous specimen trees, including oak, hickory, and cedar' plus two 19th-century magnolias east of the residence, but does not name the HALS witness tree specifically; a Feb 2026 Casey Trees article on Cedar Hill, https://caseytrees.org/2026/02/frederick-douglass-and-the-nature-at-cedar-hill/, confirms oaks are still present and that Casey Trees/NPS have an active tree-planting partnership there, but likewise does not name this specific tree). A future pass should search NPS frdo park pages directly, or a HALS DC number lookup, for a tree-specific recent confirmation before verifying. Good candidate for a future 'second DC cluster' (Anacostia/Cedar Hill) alongside the two 19th-century magnolias noted by TCLF, which are themselves unresearched leads.
leads.location_note: 1411 W Street SE, Washington, DC; Frederick Douglass National Historic Site, free, NPS-operated (though the house itself requires a timed tour, the grounds are generally open).

leads.candidate: Bur Oak and White Oak originals, U.S. Capitol Grounds (Olmsted 1874 plantings, same cohort as the verified wdc_013 Olmsted Tuliptree)
leads.why_a_lead: The Architect of the Capitol's own species table (via Olmsted Network's republished blog, olmsted.org/blog/2024/08/29/the-capitols-original-olmsted-trees, checked this pass) lists 3 surviving original Bur Oak (Quercus macrocarpa) and 2 White Oak (Quercus alba) from the same 1874-1892 Olmsted planting as the verified tulip tree, same age range (roughly 130-150 years) by definition. No individual AOC feature page (like /features/olmsted-tuliptree) was found for these species this pass; aoc.gov's general /features/trees directory page loaded via Wayback but its tree links appear to be JS-rendered and did not resolve in a plain HTML fetch. A future pass should try aoc.gov's site search or the visitthecapitol.gov/apps/grounds/trees/ interactive map (untried this pass, may be JS-heavy too) to find their exact locations, or search 'AOC Bur Oak Capitol Grounds' / 'AOC White Oak Capitol Grounds' directly for dedicated feature pages that may exist under different slugs.

leads.why_a_lead: Mentioned in passing in general cemetery writeups (search this pass) as an old oak near the chapel with local folklore ('never stops shaking its leaves'), but no source found gives species confirmation beyond 'oak', no age, no HALS or register record, and no second source. leads.candidate: Dumbarton Oaks Park (the free NPS-adjacent public park, not the private Harvard-run garden) veteran trees
leads.why_a_lead: RESOLVED this pass (the fourth attempt, first one to succeed): the American Beech Grove, HALS DC-13, verified and delivered as wdc_014 in data/research/washington-dc-verified.json. What broke the three prior failures was fetching the managing organizations' own site sections directly (TCLF's dedicated Dumbarton Oaks Park page, dopark.org's Signature Project restoration page) rather than a generic web sweep, per this pass's brief. STILL OPEN: no INDIVIDUAL named veteran specimen beyond the grove itself was found (e.g. a single named champion oak inside the park); doaks.org's own Green Garden page (checked again this pass, unchanged from prior passes) confirms the adjacent PRIVATE garden's old oaks were removed decades ago and replaced in 1928 and 2018, too young and on the paid/private side anyway. A future pass could try NPS Rock Creek Park's own tree inventory (untried directly, only its general unit pages returned 404 this pass at /rocr/learn/historyculture/dumbarton-oaks-park.htm and /rocr/planyourvisit/dumbartonoakspark.htm, so the right NPS URL slug is still unknown) for individual specimens beyond the grove.

leads.candidate: The White Oaks of the Tennis Court Garden, Tudor Place, 1644 31st Street NW, Georgetown
leads.why_a_lead: Checked this pass per the brief (Tudor Place priority 3): TCLF's Tudor Place page (independent nonprofit source) states 'In the northeast corner of the property, the Tennis Court Garden lies secluded behind a screen of white pine trees and shrubs and is framed by 200-year-old white oaks.' This is a SINGLE source for that specific claim and current living status is uncertain: Tudor Place's own site (tudorplace.org/garden/) describes a 'family of witness trees' on the estate but names only one specifically, 'the Great White Oak', which FELL in 2019 (rings counted at ~160 years) near the East Lawn tennis matches, not explicitly the same feature as TCLF's 'Tennis Court Garden'. It is unclear whether TCLF's plural 'white oaks' are a different, still-standing group, or whether TCLF's page (undated on the copy fetched) is simply stale and describing the now-fallen tree. NOT delivered: single source for the specific still-standing claim, real ambiguity about whether it duplicates the confirmed-dead Great White Oak, and paid-entry access (garden hours Tue-Sun) not yet weighed. A future pass should contact Tudor Place directly or find a second, dated source (photo, recent press) confirming which oaks, if any, still frame the Tennis Court Garden today.
leads.location_note: 1644 31st Street NW, Washington DC 20007. Garden is paid entry (self-guided visits Feb-Dec, Tue-Sat 10am-4pm, Sun noon-4pm per tudorplace.org).

leads.candidate: Oak Hill Cemetery, 3001 R Street NW, Georgetown, old trees generally
leads.why_a_lead: Checked this pass per the brief (priority 2): general web search returned only a passing, unsourced claim ('Oak Hill has some of the oldest trees in the District of Columbia... not cut down during the Civil War') with no named individual specimen, no species, no age. oakhillcemeterydc.org's own site (fetched directly this pass) has no historic-tree content at all, only a modern 'Memorial Tree Program' for burial plantings, unrelated to old/remarkable trees. No TCLF entry found for Oak Hill Cemetery specifically in the time available. Not pursued further: no named candidate to verify against two sources. A future pass would need to start from a different source entirely, e.g. the cemetery's own published historic preservation plan or a dedicated DC tree survey, since neither the cemetery's own site nor general search names a specific tree.

leads.name: Lafayette Park / President's Park (unnamed specimens)

location.neighbourhood: Lafayette Square, President's Park, directly north of the White House

sources: Jon Pattee, Rock Creek Conservancy, by email 2026-08-11
leads.why_not_published: READER TIP, not yet researched. Jon Pattee replied to our own question with 'There are several lovely ones in the park in front of the White House!' That is Lafayette Square, seven acres of President's Park, cleared and planted after the Revolutionary War and landscaped by Andrew Jackson Downing in 1851-52, and we publish nothing in it. Needs a pass to identify WHICH trees: NPS designates witness trees here and Casey Trees has written about DC's. Two things make it cheap and worth doing: it is NPS ground, so photographs by federal staff are public domain, which is the standing answer to Washington's photo gap (13 of our 14 DC trees have none); and it is the most walkable spot in the city, steps from wdc_004, wdc_005, wdc_008 and wdc_009 on the Mall. DO NOT use the Jackson Magnolia: it stood on the White House grounds rather than the park, and it was removed in 2025, so it fails the living-tree rule.

leads.candidate: Chinese Hackberry (Celtis sinensis), Donald W. Reynolds Center for American Art and Portraiture, 8th and F Streets NW, Penn Quarter
leads.why_a_lead: Found 2026-09-23 while hunting a fifth National Mall tree. Smithsonian Gardens calls it planted 1900-1910 and thought to be one of the largest and oldest of its species in the district, sprawling over the Reynolds Center's grounds. Not on the Mall, so it does not help the park page, and a second independent source was not found in this pass; Smithsonian Gardens is the only account we have. Worth a verify pass: the grounds are open public ground, the tree is accessioned in their tree collection, and it would be the first Celtis we map in the US. Start at gardens.si.edu's tree collection pages.

verified_entry.verify_notes:
FLAGGED: one source (NPS), US one-source rule.
- NPS notable-trees layer, feature 'Lincoln Elm': 'Near the Lincoln Memorial, a few elms survive from the first phases of planting in the 1920s... Between the Lincoln Memorial and the Korean War Memorial is one outstanding American elm about 100 years in age. The tree has the classic form of a mature elm; its main branches sweeping and curving upwards before descending in elegant lines. A recent storm tore off one of its branches.' The planned planting was a double semicircle of elms east of the memorial, scaled back to an alternating design; at the time many elms were dedicated as memorial trees. Elms around the memorial are of many ages (healthy distribution); NPS arborists prune against Dutch elm disease.
- NPS Silent Sentinels article (fetched): in 1921 American Forests sponsored a memorial planting campaign and First Lady Florence Harding planted two American elms at the 23rd Street entrance to the Lincoln Memorial grounds for the armistice that ended WWI. The article does NOT say this outstanding elm is one of those two; do not claim it. Age is NPS's 'about 100 years', no tree-specific planting record.
- No girth or height published. Layer point (38.88819,-77.04888) is NPS's placement for the tree, but many elms stand here; approximate. The layer's own image of it carries 'non-commercial use only', so not a photo candidate.
- Alive: NPS storymap text is current (recent storm branch loss mentioned); lifecheck RECENT hit (iNat 2025-01-20) is only a generic nearby observation, not this trunk.
- Photo: Commons geosearch within 150 m returned no tree photo that identifies this elm; none recorded.
- Neighbours: the Willow Oak Circle (wdc_009) is about 100 m north-east. A photo or on-site GPS would settle which elm; the page can ask the reader.

verified_entry.verify_notes:
FLAGGED: one source family, the owner of the ground (Historic Congressional Cemetery, a 501(c)(3)); US one-source rule and owner-of-ground rule. Arboretum accreditation reported by Hill Rag 2026-10-18.
- Arboretum page (fetched 2026-10-22): 'HCC's swamp oak is over 120 years old, having been documented in photographs from 1913 as a young, established tree.' Designated WITNESS TREE ('has lived for over a century and has been a witness to cemetery history'). Max height for species 95 ft, max age 300 yrs (species figures, not this tree).
- Cemetery blog 2026-09-01 (fetched): 'The large swamp white oak near the gates of the cemetery. Historical images place it as at least 113 years old. It is a large specimen for its age.' Photo credited 2026 (Vincent Vassal), so alive in 2026.
- CONFLICT: the tree-sponsorship page (a fundraising page) calls it 'a designated Witness Tree pre-dating the Civil War'; the arboretum page and blog rest on the 1913 photographs. Use 'over a century' (1913 photograph, young established tree) and do not claim pre-Civil War.
- No girth or height measured for this tree published. Species is rare as an old specimen in DC cemetery planting; 'a large specimen for its age' is the cemetery's own wording.
- Pin: the cemetery says 'near the gates'; coordinate is the 1801 E St SE address point (Nominatim, 38.8826554,-76.9788787), NOT the trunk. Approximate, cemetery gate level. Cemetery is 35 acres so not a small site. An on-site GPS fix or the cemetery's Tree Walk map would settle it.

location.neighbourhood: Arlington (Virginia), about 35 minutes from downtown DC by Metro (Orange/Silver/Blue Line to Rosslyn, then about a 20 minute walk north-west)

leads.access: Free. Fort C.F. Smith is an Arlington County park and historic site; the tree stands inside it, in a steep wooded ravine.
leads.verify_notes: One source, but the owner of the ground: Arlington County. The county's Specimen Trees page says: currently the largest tree measured in Arlington County, almost 21 feet in circumference and 140 feet tall, likely one of few trees at the historic park to pre-date the Civil War. The county nomination form (Owner: Arlington County, nominator Urban Forestry Commission) says the same, adds County Champion tulip poplar, and 'grows in a steep wooded ravine and may have provided shade to Union soldiers stationed at the fort'. girth_cm 635 is 'almost 21 ft' converted (21 ft = 640); height_m 42.7 is 140 ft. Neither page carries a measurement date and no age figure is given, so age_min 160 only restates 'pre-dates the Civil War' (1861-65) as a floor; no upper bound. Do not call it a state champion: a search summary claimed one for a different tree. Pin: the park centre only (Nominatim, park bbox about 250 m by 300 m); no OSM tree node and no register coordinate exist, so precision is approximate at park level and the tree is NOT findable by pin: it fails findable unless a trunk photo or the park's staff gives the spot. Recognition line to use: the biggest tree in the ravine below the fort. Alive: only an undated 'currently'. Transit: Rosslyn Metro about 12 minutes from Metro Center plus a 20 minute walk, so about 35 minutes door to door, slightly over.
leads.reason: Verified (Arlington County is the owner and source; almost 21 ft girth, 140 ft, pre-Civil War, County Champion) but only a park-level pin and no photo, so it fails the findable rule (park is not a small site). Held here as a lead with its full record; ships the moment a trunk coordinate or photo is found. About 35 min from downtown DC (Rosslyn Metro plus 20 min walk).
